title: KV cache stale-read hunt and robust recovery
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Follow-up ticket from a recent incident where under sustained load and aggressive eviction the KV/prefix cache returned stale entries for live keys for a short window. The stale reads caused quality regressions and occasional increased tail latency as downstream repair logic retried. This ticket coordinates hunt, short-term mitigations, long-term fixes, telemetry additions, and runbook updates.
incident_summary: On 2026-02-08 we observed a capacity spike that triggered an eviction storm. Several hosts reported short-lived stale reads where callers received older values after a successful write/refresh. The effect lasted seconds per-key but was visible in QA evals and correlated with increased client retries and token-level quality regressions.
timeline: 2026-02-08 03:12 UTC - Alerts triggered for increased cache miss rate and retry loops; 03:18 - on-call rotated and initial mitigation (throttle aggressive eviction) applied; 03:40 - rollback of an earlier micro-optimizing commit suspected to amplify races; 04:05 - temporary guardrail deployed to disable background compaction on affected nodes. Investigation continued over the following days focused on eviction/insert races and generation counters.
root_cause: A race between the slab allocator's free/compaction path and the hash-index update path allowed a recently-freed slab slot to be reallocated while a stale index pointer still referenced the old slot for a small time window. Because entries were not versioned at lookup, a stale pointer could return a previously-evicted value until the tombstone propagation finished. This was exacerbated by aggressive concurrent eviction heuristics under capacity pressure and a missed assertion in the write path that would have prevented reuse during in-flight lookups.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Disable aggressive background compaction on affected pools (rolled at 03:40). 2) Add a short (1s) per-slab quiesce window before reuse to avoid immediate reuse races. 3) Deploy a temporary detection hook that rejects values which fail a lightweight checksum when generation mismatch suspected.
long_term_plan: 1) Introduce per-entry generation/version counters and include them in index lookups so stale pointers fail fast. 2) Replace implicit tombstone timing assumptions with explicit state transitions (VALID -> PENDING_FREE -> FREE) guarded by atomic ops. 3) Expand unit and stress tests (including fault-injection/chaos tests) to exercise eviction/insert races at scale. 4) Rework slab allocator to avoid immediate reuse without explicit handoff. 5) Formal rollout: canary -> 20% -> 100% with automated rollback on regressions.
telemetry_changes: 1) Emit per-key generation mismatches and tombstone hits as a dedicated metric. 2) Add histogram of time-between-evict-and-reuse per-slab. 3) Track correlation between eviction rate and client retry rate. 4) Add a dashboard showing stale-read alarms, with alert thresholds tuned to detect even small infrequent occurrences.
runbook_updates: 1) Add 'stale-read' triage checklist with steps to disable compaction and increase per-slab quiesce. 2) Document diagnostic queries and flamegraphs to identify hosts with high tombstone propagation. 3) Define rollback criteria for generation-version rollout. 4) Add contact list (owners) for runtime, allocator, and infra teams.

notes: Decision log: prefer versioned entries over global eviction locks because locks materially increase tail latency under bursty traffic.
Trade-offs: generation/version adds extra metadata per entry (~8-16B) which increases memory pressure; mitigation includes compacted meta-layout and optional sampling in low-memory tiers.
Reviewer feedback: PM and SRE prefer conservative canary thresholds and an initial detection-only rollout to avoid customer-visible regressions.
Next steps: complete telemetry and chaos tests before merging generation-counter change; schedule a 30-minute post-canary review to validate metrics.
